paragraphs: This paper studies what makes a useful representation for reinforcement learning by examining the geometry of value functions. A value function describes the cumulative reward associated with following a policy. The authors consider representations that support accurate linear approximations of the value functions of all stationary policies in a given environment, rather than tailoring the representation to just one policy.

The central theoretical result reduces this broad representation objective to predicting a special class of functions called adversarial value functions, or AVFs. This gives a more focused target for representation learning: a particular collection of value predictions can capture what matters for the larger objective.

The authors also show that using value prediction as an auxiliary learning task corresponds to an expected-error relaxation of their formulation. AVFs emerge as natural candidates for these auxiliary tasks, with a close connection to proto-value functions. Experiments in the four-room domain illustrate their characteristics and usefulness, complementing the formal argument for learning representations through value prediction.
neurips-2019-a-geometric-perspective-on-.tldr: A geometric analysis identifies adversarial value functions as useful targets for learning reinforcement-learning representations.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning requires assigning agents to tasks in ways that support coordinated behavior. Centralized reinforcement learning can solve small instances, but scaling and transferring the learned behavior to different scenarios are difficult. This paper focuses on problems with an intrinsic notion of locality, where interactions between agents and tasks are limited, for example by geographic proximity.

The proposed approach learns a scoring model and uses its scores inside a centralized optimization problem. Solving that problem at each step produces the agent-to-task assignment. Different combinations of scoring models and optimization procedures represent increasingly complex coordination patterns, making the assignment itself a structured prediction problem.

The locality assumption enables a policy learned on small instances to be reused on larger ones without additional training. Experiments cover a toy search-and-rescue problem and target selection in StarCraft: Brood War. On instances with five times as many agents and tasks as those used for training, the method significantly outperforms strong rule-based baselines, supporting its claimed ability to transfer coordination behavior across problem sizes.
neurips-2019-a-structured-prediction-app.tldr: Learned assignment scores and centralized optimization let locally interacting agent teams transfer coordination policies to larger problems.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks while retaining what it learned on earlier ones. This paper proposes an incremental approach that combines three operations: compressing a deep model, selecting critical weights, and progressively expanding the network. These operations are integrated repeatedly as tasks arrive in sequence.

The combination addresses both memory of previous tasks and the size of the resulting model. Expansion provides capacity for additional learning, while compression and weight selection help maintain compactness. The authors present this coordinated process as a method that can scale with the number of sequential tasks and avoid forgetting previously learned tasks.

The approach also uses accumulated knowledge to support new learning. The authors show that their compaction and selection/expansion mechanism can produce better models for new tasks than training separate models independently. Experimental results demonstrate a deep model handling multiple tasks without forgetting while remaining compact and achieving more satisfactory performance than individual-task training. The stated contribution is therefore a way to combine retention, reuse, and controlled model growth within one continual-learning procedure.
neurips-2019-compacting-picking-and-grow.tldr: Repeated compression, critical-weight selection, and network expansion support continual learning without forgetting while maintaining compact models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much parallel gradient computation can accelerate non-smooth convex optimization. In the sequential setting, gradient descent is optimal when the number of computed gradients is smaller than the problem dimension. The authors instead consider an oracle that can answer a number of gradient queries polynomial in the dimension during each round.

They show that gradient descent remains optimal only up to roughly the square root of the dimension in interaction rounds, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Their lower bound strengthens an earlier construction that established optimality only up to the cube root of the dimension. The result identifies a larger range in which even extensive parallel querying cannot improve on gradient descent's round complexity.

Beyond the square-root regime, where gradient descent was already known to be suboptimal, the authors propose a method with improved complexity. Its analysis extends results on acceleration for highly smooth convex optimization. They conjecture that this new method is optimal; that final optimality claim is a conjecture rather than a proved conclusion.
neurips-2019-complexity-of-highly-parall.tldr: The paper sharpens limits on parallel non-smooth convex optimization and proposes a faster method beyond gradient descent's optimal regime.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization algorithms can be studied through differential equations that describe related continuous-time dynamics. These equations make it possible to analyze convergence using Lyapunov functions, which track progress toward a solution. The practical challenge is converting a continuous flow into discrete computational steps while preserving the convergence behavior established for that flow.

This paper uses opportunistic state-triggered control to choose variable step sizes for forward-Euler discretization. The step-size design draws directly on the Lyapunov functions used to analyze the original differential equations. In this way, the same mathematical description of progress guides how the continuous dynamics are turned into an algorithm.

The resulting discretizations preserve the Lyapunov decay of the original dynamics, connecting the continuous convergence analysis to discrete updates. This matters because a useful continuous-time rate must survive discretization to inform an implementable method. The authors also suggest that the design philosophy may work with integration schemes other than forward Euler, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility rather than an established result for every scheme.
neurips-2019-convergence-rate-matching-d.tldr: Lyapunov-guided variable step sizes turn accelerated continuous optimization flows into discrete updates that preserve their Lyapunov decay.

paragraphs: Feature-importance methods help users understand how inputs influence a predictive model's output. For high-dimensional inputs, producing accurate explanations quickly is challenging, and the reliability of those explanations also matters. CXPlain approaches explanation as a causal learning task, training a separate model to estimate how inputs cause outputs within the predictive model being explained.

Once trained, the explanation model can provide feature-importance estimates quickly. The method also uses bootstrap ensembling to quantify uncertainty in those estimates. This adds information about how dependable an explanation may be, alongside the estimated importance of each input. The causal framing concerns the behavior of the target machine-learning model.

The reported experiments find CXPlain significantly faster and more accurate than existing model-agnostic feature-importance methods. They also find a strong correlation between the ensembles' uncertainty estimates and their ability to estimate importance accurately on held-out data. Together, these findings support learning an explanation model as a practical way to obtain both efficient explanations and useful signals about explanation reliability.
neurips-2019-cxplain-causal-explanations.tldr: CXPlain learns fast feature-importance explanations and uses bootstrap ensembles to estimate their uncertainty.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select representative points from a dataset by learning from datasets with known summaries. Its framework uses a facility-location objective to select representatives, while learning a data representation that makes those selections agree with the ground-truth summaries. The representation and the selection rule are therefore connected through a supervised learning objective.

Because the underlying selection problem is NP-hard, the authors study a convex relaxation based on sparse representation. They identify conditions under which solving the relaxed problem recovers the desired representatives. A specially designed loss encourages the representation network to satisfy those conditions, linking summary recovery to explicit theoretical requirements.

Learning the representation still involves a non-convex loss. The proposed training scheme alternates between updating the representation with point-to-representative assignments fixed and updating those assignments using the current representation. Recovery guarantees depend on satisfying the stated conditions. Experiments on identifying key steps in instructional videos show improvements over state-of-the-art supervised subset-selection algorithms, demonstrating the framework's usefulness for learning representative subactivities.
neurips-2019-deep-supervised-summarizati.tldr: The method learns representations that support theoretically grounded representative selection and improves key-step summarization of instructional videos.

paragraphs: This paper considers selecting training examples from multiple private datasets to match a target task represented by a small validation set. The source and target data may have substantially different input distributions. The selection objective minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy, a measure of statistical distance, between the chosen summary and the target validation data.

The authors work in a privacy model where a trusted curator coordinates selection while accessing as little private information as possible. Their protocol limits curator access to O(K^(1/3)|D_s| + |D_v|) points, where K is the number of sources and the two set sizes describe the summary and validation data. It also provides formal privacy guarantees for information leakage between data owners.

The protocol combines two hash functions, drawing on random features and differential privacy mechanisms, and introduces a differentially private auctioning procedure described as noiseless. Its quality closely matches the best known non-private greedy method while adding strong privacy guarantees. Experiments on real-world datasets support the protocol's effectiveness, connecting the theoretical guarantees to the proposed distributed summarization task.
neurips-2019-differentially-private-dist.tldr: A distributed protocol selects target-relevant data summaries with strong privacy guarantees and limited access by a trusted curator.

paragraphs: Architecture search for object detection is expensive because candidate detectors typically require ImageNet pretraining, while training from scratch needs more epochs. This paper proposes Neural Architecture Transformation Search, or NATS, to adapt an existing classification network for detection. The search begins with an existing network and reuses its learned weights.

NATS searches for channel-level transformations within a space designed specifically for object detection. Its gradient-based procedure discovers how to transform the architecture rather than constructing an entire network. Pretrained weights remain usable during both search and retraining, making weight reuse a central source of efficiency throughout the process.

The transformed network requires no additional parameters or floating-point operations and is described as suitable for hardware optimization and real-time use. Experiments apply the method to ResNet and ResNeXt networks with various detection frameworks. The reported COCO results show significant improvements while retaining speed. These findings support architecture transformation as a practical way to adapt classification networks to detection without increasing their stated parameter and computation requirements.
neurips-2019-efficient-neural-architectu.tldr: NATS efficiently adapts pretrained classification networks for object detection through channel-level transformations without adding parameters or FLOPs.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model sequences of discrete events through an intensity function describing how event occurrence varies over time. Existing recurrent neural network models often restrict this function to a particular shape, such as exponential growth or decay since the latest event. Those assumptions can limit the event patterns the model can express.

The paper changes which quantity the neural network represents directly. A feedforward network models the integral of the intensity function, and differentiation then produces the intensity itself. This construction allows a more general time dependence while keeping the integral readily available for evaluating the model's likelihood.

That combination matters because the log-likelihood requires the integrated intensity as well as the intensity. The proposed approach evaluates it exactly without numerical approximations, while retaining a flexible intensity model within an RNN-based framework. On both synthetic and real datasets, the authors report performance competitive with or superior to previous state-of-the-art methods. The findings support modeling the integral as a way to combine expressive event dynamics with tractable likelihood evaluation.
neurips-2019-fully-neural-network-based-.tldr: Modeling integrated event intensity with a neural network enables flexible temporal point processes and exact log-likelihood evaluation.

paragraphs: Lasso-type regression methods face a tuning problem: the best regularization strength depends on an unknown noise level. Concomitant estimators address this by estimating noise and regression coefficients together. This paper also considers repeated measurements, which are often averaged to reduce noise variance but thereby lose sample size and information needed for more detailed noise modeling.

The proposed estimator works with measurements before averaging and can accommodate complex noise structure. Its data-fitting term comes from smoothing the nuclear norm. This provides a mathematical route to incorporating the available repeated observations while jointly addressing regression and noise estimation.

The resulting optimization problem is convex. Smoothing theory makes it compatible with advanced optimization methods that exploit sparse solutions, connecting the richer noise model to practical computation. The authors demonstrate benefits on toy datasets, realistic simulations, and real neuroimaging data. The contribution is a combination of noise-aware estimation and tractable sparse optimization that preserves information otherwise discarded by averaging, with practical support across the stated experimental settings.
neurips-2019-handling-correlated-and-rep.tldr: A convex concomitant estimator uses unaveraged repeated measurements to fit sparse regression models while handling complex noise.

paragraphs: Network embeddings represent vertices as compact vectors that retain useful information for later tasks. In textual networks, that information includes both text associated with vertices and the links between them. This paper proposes Variational Homophilic Embedding, or VHE, as a generative framework for bringing these two sources of information into the same representation.

VHE models textual meaning with a variational autoencoder and incorporates network structure through a specially designed prior. The prior expresses homophily by encouraging connected vertices to have similar embedding vectors. Text and connectivity therefore shape the learned representations through different, coordinated parts of the probabilistic model.

The design encourages generalization to downstream tasks, robustness when observations are incomplete, and the ability to represent previously unseen vertices. Experiments on real-world networks across multiple tasks report consistently better performance than competing state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the usefulness of combining generative text modeling with a structural prior, while the generalization and robustness benefits are presented as properties encouraged by that formulation.
neurips-2019-improving-textual-network-l.tldr: VHE combines generative text modeling with a prior favoring similar embeddings for connected vertices to improve textual network learning.

paragraphs: Quadratic regression includes products of input features so that a prediction can depend on their interactions. These terms can improve accuracy, but p original features create a problem with order p squared possible terms. Seeking a sparse set of useful interactions helps statistically, yet finding that set can still require substantial time and memory.

Interaction Hard Thresholding, or IntHT, modifies iterative hard thresholding to exploit the special structure of quadratic terms. It approximately extracts the largest entries of a gradient with p squared components using sub-quadratic time and space. This targets the computational bottleneck without requiring a full-sized gradient search.

Under standard high-dimensional sparse recovery assumptions, the authors prove that the method converges linearly to a consistent estimate despite its computational approximations. Synthetic experiments demonstrate its value. Numerical results also suggest extension to higher-order regression, while a variance-reduced stochastic variant receives theoretical analysis. The main contribution is a provably accurate sparse quadratic regression algorithm whose time and memory requirements grow more slowly than the full interaction space.
neurips-2019-interaction-hard-thresholdi.tldr: IntHT exploits quadratic structure to recover sparse feature interactions in sub-quadratic time and space under sparse recovery assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper estimates treatment effects that vary across individuals when unobserved confounders are present, using a valid instrument. One motivating setting randomizes a recommendation or opportunity to act, while the desired effect concerns the action itself. The randomized intervention and the downstream treatment therefore play different roles in the estimation problem.

The authors reduce effect estimation to minimizing a loss that depends on auxiliary prediction models. This allows flexible machine-learning methods, including neural networks and forests, to fit the effect model. The loss satisfies Neyman orthogonality, providing robustness to errors in estimating those auxiliary models.

The framework can also estimate projections of the true effect onto simpler model classes. For parametric classes, the parameter estimates are asymptotically normal, enabling confidence sets. Applications include estimating membership's effect on webpage engagement using an intent-to-treat experiment involving four million travel-site users. Synthetic data and public schooling-and-income datasets provide additional validation. The contribution connects flexible prediction tools to causal estimation with explicit robustness and inference properties, with a valid instrument remaining central to the setting.
neurips-2019-machine-learning-estimation.tldr: An orthogonal learning objective enables flexible estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects with valid instruments and robustness to auxiliary-model errors.

paragraphs: A universal value function approximator predicts cumulative rewards for different combinations of starting states and goals. Estimating values for distant goals is empirically difficult and can lead to unsuccessful policies. This paper addresses that difficulty in large Markov decision processes with sparse rewards, where both exploration and routing between remote states are challenging.

The method represents the environment hierarchically. A dynamic map of landmark states provides a high-level description of the visited state space, while a low-level value network supplies precise local decisions. This separates the broad problem of navigating across the environment from the more local decisions needed along the way.

Landmarks are selected from past experience using farthest point sampling. The authors report that this improves exploration compared with uniform sampling. Experiments show agents reaching distant goals early in training and outperforming standard reinforcement-learning algorithms on several challenging tasks. The findings support using an explicit landmark map to complement local value estimation when long-range value predictions are difficult to learn directly.
neurips-2019-mapping-state-space-using-l.tldr: A dynamic landmark map combined with local value estimation helps agents explore and reach distant goals in sparse-reward environments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models are used for inference, parameter estimation, sampling, and likelihood evaluation, but practical methods often trade off these capabilities. Fenchel Mini-Max Learning, or FML, proposes a framework intended to accommodate all four. Its starting point is classical maximum likelihood estimation, with particular attention to models whose normalizing constant is computationally intractable.

The authors reformulate maximum likelihood as a minimax game. The resulting training objective is unbiased and does not explicitly involve the difficult normalizing constant. It is also suitable for stochastic gradient descent, connecting the probabilistic estimation objective to an optimization procedure that can operate through stochastic updates.

This reformulation addresses a longstanding obstacle to unbiased estimation of unnormalized statistical models. The authors demonstrate the framework on learning such models, nonparametric density estimation, and generative-model training, reporting encouraging empirical results. The stated advance is a common learning formulation that preserves an unbiased objective while supporting several probabilistic modeling goals, with the experiments illustrating its utility across the three applications.
neurips-2019-on-fenchel-mini-max-learnin.tldr: FML reformulates maximum likelihood as a minimax game with an unbiased stochastic training objective that avoids explicit intractable normalization.

paragraphs: Many classification goals depend on nonlinear combinations of aggregate classification rates. Examples include F-measure and G-mean, as well as constraints involving predictive parity, distribution divergences, or churn ratios. This paper develops a common optimization framework for a broad class of such objectives and constraints, including metrics that do not decompose into separate losses for individual examples.

The method extends two-player game formulations of constrained learning to a three-player game. The additional player decouples classifier rates from the nonlinear objective, and training seeks an equilibrium of the resulting game. This separation generalizes existing algorithms and permits new ones with more flexibility in handling nonlinear rate constraints.

The authors establish convergence guarantees for convex functions of rates and describe an extension to sums of rate ratios. Those guarantees retain the stated convexity qualification; they do not establish convergence for every nonlinear metric. Experiments on multiple fairness tasks support the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a reusable game-based formulation that links aggregate performance goals and constraints to trainable classifiers.
neurips-2019-optimizing-generalized-rate.tldr: A three-player game separates classifier rates from nonlinear objectives to optimize aggregate metrics and constraints more flexibly.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning guarantees for losses that may have heavy tails, where unusually large loss values can matter substantially. It uses the PAC-Bayesian framework to derive a robust estimator of risk and a learning algorithm based on that estimator. The estimator is designed to be easy to compute, connecting the theoretical argument to a usable learning procedure.

The analysis produces a new optimal Gibbs posterior with finite-sample excess-risk bounds whose confidence dependence is logarithmic. An excess-risk bound describes how far the learned model's risk is from the comparison target. A finite-sample result provides such control without relying only on behavior in the limit of unlimited data.

The central distributional assumption is that the first three moments of the loss distribution are bounded. Under that assumption, the resulting algorithm achieves statistical error that is nearly sub-Gaussian, with a qualification depending on the quality of the prior. Thus the result provides strong error control for potentially heavy-tailed losses while retaining explicit moment and prior-quality conditions.
neurips-2019-pac-bayes-under-potentially.tldr: A computable robust PAC-Bayesian estimator yields nearly sub-Gaussian error under bounded first three loss moments, subject to prior quality.

paragraphs: Principal component projection and regression restrict computation to the top eigenspace associated with a data matrix. These are basic operations in machine learning, optimization, and numerical analysis. This paper studies how to perform them efficiently when the matrix has many rows, focusing on the computational cost of obtaining the projection or regression result.

The authors provide algorithms with nearly linear running time for a fixed eigenvalue distribution and large row count. This improves on previous approaches that had superlinear running times when either the number of top eigenvalues or the gap between eigenspaces was large. The conditions on the eigenvalue distribution and matrix size are part of the stated result.

The method uses rational polynomial approximations to transform the original tasks into asymmetric linear-system problems. A variant of stochastic variance-reduced gradient, or SVRG, solves those systems. Preliminary empirical experiments corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore an algorithmic reduction that brings these spectral tasks within nearly linear time in the specified regime, with initial experimental support.
neurips-2019-principal-component-project.tldr: Rational approximations and an asymmetric SVRG solver enable nearly linear-time principal component projection and regression in the stated spectral regime.

paragraphs: Private stochastic convex optimization aims to minimize population loss using independent, identically distributed samples while satisfying differential privacy. The paper assumes convex, Lipschitz loss functions. Much previous work tightly characterized excess loss on the observed sample, but bounds for the underlying population remained substantially less precise.

The authors show that, up to logarithmic factors, optimal private excess population loss equals the larger of two quantities: optimal non-private excess population loss and optimal private excess empirical loss. This relates the cost of learning from finite data to the cost of protecting privacy, giving a sharp characterization of their combined effect.

In the parameter regime the authors describe as most common in practice, private optimization consequently achieves the same asymptotic 1/sqrt(n) rate as non-private optimization. The previous best result in that setting was 1/n^(1/4). The approach builds on existing private algorithms and analyzes their stability to establish generalization. The matching rate is tied to the specified regime, while the broader maximum-of-two-quantities result describes the tradeoff more generally.
neurips-2019-private-stochastic-convex-o.tldr: Sharp population-loss bounds show private convex optimization can match the non-private 1/sqrt(n) rate in a practically common parameter regime.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing is a scalable way to construct neural classifiers with provable robustness to adversarial perturbations measured in the l2 norm. This paper seeks to improve the performance of those smoothed classifiers through adversarial training. The focus is on strengthening robustness that can be certified, within the stated perturbation model.

The authors design an attack adapted specifically to smoothed classifiers and use it during adversarial training. Aligning the training attack with the smoothed classifier provides a way to improve the classifier whose robustness will be evaluated. They show how this combination boosts provable robustness rather than treating smoothing and adversarial training as separate procedures.

Extensive experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 report consistent, significant improvements over the existing provably l2-robust classifiers considered in the paper. The authors also find that pretraining and semi-supervised learning improve the adversarially trained smoothed classifiers further. These findings establish the reported state of the art for provable l2 defenses and show that additional learning strategies can strengthen the combined approach.
neurips-2019-provably-robust-deep-learni.tldr: Adversarial training with an attack tailored to smoothed classifiers improves their provable l2 robustness on ImageNet and CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: Learning to plan directly from observations is promising, but long-horizon performance can be limited by prediction-model accuracy. Classical symbolic planners handle long tasks well, yet require predefined symbolic rules and states. Regression Planning Networks, or RPN, combine elements of both approaches to produce long-term symbolic plans conditioned on high-dimensional observations.

RPN uses regression planning, meaning that it reasons backward from the desired task goal. The network generates a sequence of intermediate goals that works back toward the current observation. This gives the learned planner a goal-directed structure drawn from classical planning while allowing it to learn from visual inputs end to end.

The authors show that the model retains useful symbolic-planning traits, including solving tasks not encountered during training. Evaluations use a grid world and a simulated three-dimensional kitchen with complex visual scenes and long task horizons. RPN achieves near-optimal performance on completely new task instances in those settings. The findings support backward intermediate-goal generation as a way to connect visual learning with longer-term planning and task generalization.
neurips-2019-regression-planning-network.tldr: RPN learns to plan backward through intermediate goals, producing long-term symbolic plans from visual observations and generalizing to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: This paper proposes training neural networks while progressively growing their architecture. Growth occurs by splitting existing neurons into multiple offspring, so the structure can adapt during learning. The central questions are which neurons to split and how to update the new neurons so that the structural change improves the optimization process.

The authors derive a criterion for selecting the best subset of neurons to split and a splitting gradient for updating their offspring. Both come from a functional steepest-descent perspective, which treats architectural changes as part of the optimization problem. This gives the growth operation a mathematical basis alongside ordinary parameter training.

The theoretical analysis characterizes splitting as second-order functional steepest descent for escaping saddle points in an L-infinity Wasserstein metric space. In that same setting, standard parameter gradient descent is a first-order method. The authors present the resulting strategy as computationally efficient architecture optimization, particularly useful for learning lightweight networks under resource constraints. The contribution is a principled way to select and direct network growth.
neurips-2019-splitting-steepest-descent-.tldr: A functional steepest-descent rule selects neurons to split and directs their offspring, enabling principled growth of lightweight neural architectures.

paragraphs: Scattering transforms are deep convolutional representations with fixed, non-trainable components built around wavelets at multiple scales. Their appeal includes mathematical stability: suitable small changes in the data domain produce controlled changes in the representation. Extending this idea to network data is challenging because graph topology gives the domain an irregular structure where ordinary convolutions do not directly apply.

The paper constructs graph scattering transforms using multiresolution graph wavelets. These wavelets can be computed through graph convolutions, providing the basic operations needed to carry the scattering architecture onto networks. The result preserves the multiscale representation idea while adapting its computations to the graph domain.

The authors prove stability to metric perturbations of the underlying network. This supports robustness when network topology changes within the setting covered by the analysis. They identify transfer learning, topology estimation, and time-varying graphs as particularly relevant uses. The main finding is a theoretical stability guarantee for graph-based representations, giving a mathematical reason to expect controlled sensitivity to changes in their underlying network.
neurips-2019-stability-of-graph-scatteri.tldr: Multiresolution graph wavelets extend scattering transforms to networks with proven stability to metric perturbations of the underlying graph.

paragraphs: Large forecasting datasets can contain many correlated time series that evolve together. A model may train on the whole collection yet predict each series mainly from its own past, leaving cross-series information underused. DeepGLO addresses this by combining a global model of shared patterns with a local model of each individual series.

Its global component uses matrix factorization regularized by a temporal convolution network. A second temporal network captures local behavior and associated covariates. Together, these components connect collection-wide structure with series-specific prediction. The authors also state that the model can train effectively on diverse series with substantially different scales without prior normalization or rescaling.

Empirical results show that DeepGLO can outperform state-of-the-art forecasting approaches. On one public dataset with more than 100,000 time-series dimensions, the reported improvement in weighted absolute percentage error exceeds 25% over other methods. That result illustrates the potential benefit of combining global dependence and local calibration, while remaining a finding for the reported dataset rather than a guaranteed improvement on every forecasting problem.
neurips-2019-think-globally-act-locally-.tldr: DeepGLO combines global matrix factorization with local temporal modeling to improve forecasting across large collections of correlated time series.
